think:
1. Core Clinical Tension: A 72-year-old postmenopausal woman presenting routinely for symptomatic stage III uterine prolapse is incidentally found on transvaginal ultrasonography to harbor a large (9 cm) multilocular right adnexal mass with solid mural components and acoustic shadowing. In an elderly postmenopausal patient, such complex multilocular adnexal masses strongly suggest an ovarian epithelial malignancy or borderline cystadenoma, making an isolated primary ovarian hydatid cyst completely unexpected.
2. Admission Breakpoint: The breakpoint occurs following outpatient gynecological examination, normal baseline laboratory tests (renal/liver panels, CA-125, CEA), and transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrating the 9-cm multilocular adnexal mass with a 1.4% calculated ADNEX malignancy risk, immediately prior to laparoscopic surgical intervention.
3. Differential Distinctions: Ovarian epithelial malignancy was the primary preoperative concern given the patient's postmenopausal status and multilocular sonographic architecture with solid components; however, serum CA-125 and CEA were normal, the IOTA ADNEX model showed low malignancy risk, and intraoperative frozen section formally excluded malignant cells. Benign ovarian cystadenoma was considered due to the multicystic nature, but histopathology demonstrated diagnostic parasitic laminated membranes and germinal tissue. Postoperative CT confirmed absence of hepatic or pulmonary cysts, validating primary ovarian localization.
case_prompt: A 72-year-old postmenopausal woman is referred to the outpatient gynecology clinic for evaluation of suspected uterine prolapse. Her medical history includes three uncomplicated vaginal deliveries, menopause at age 52, and chronic essential hypertension managed with valsartan; she does not smoke and has no history of jaundice, hepatic disease, or prior abdominal surgeries. At age 62, an abnormal Pap smear showing low-grade squamous intraepithelial lesion with negative HPV DNA testing resolved with unremarkable subsequent cervical surveillance. On physical examination, body mass index is 28 kg/m² and stage III pelvic organ prolapse (POP-Q) is confirmed. Vital signs are normal: temperature 36.2°C, heart rate 68 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/75 mm Hg, respiratory rate 18 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 100% on ambient air. Serum hepatic panels, renal function tests, and plain chest radiography are normal. Transvaginal ultrasonography demonstrates a multilocular cystic tumor under the right adnexa measuring up to 9 cm in maximum diameter, containing solid components measuring under 7 mm and acoustic shadowing, with unremarkable findings in the uterus and left adnexa. Serum CEA and CA-125 levels are within normal limits, with an International Ovarian Tumor Analysis (IOTA) ADNEX model calculating a 1.4% probability of malignancy.

diagnostic_reasoning.candidate: Malignant ovarian neoplasm / epithelial ovarian carcinoma
diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A 9-cm multilocular adnexal mass containing solid components in a 72-year-old postmenopausal woman strongly suggested primary ovarian carcinoma, but CA-125 and CEA were normal, the IOTA ADNEX calculated risk was low (1.4%), and intraoperative frozen section formally ruled out malignancy.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: Using the International Ovarian Tumor Analysis (IOTA) ADNEX model, we calculated a low risk of malignancy 1.4%... A frozen section study of the right adnexa ruled out malignancy

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: A benign mucinous or serous cystadenoma was considered due to the multicystic appearance with internal septations, but surgical histopathology demonstrated characteristic parasitic cuticular and germinal membranes of a hydatid cyst rather than an epithelial neoplasm.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The histopathology specimen revealed a hydatid cyst of the ovary.

diagnostic_reasoning.rule_out_reason: Definitive histopathologic examination of the resected adnexal specimen revealed an isolated ovarian hydatid cyst, with postoperative abdominal CT confirming complete absence of hepatic or pulmonary involvement and establishing primary ovarian echinococcosis.
diagnostic_reasoning.quote: The histopathology specimen revealed a hydatid cyst of the ovary. Additionally, a postoperative abdominal Computed Tomography (CT) revealed no other sites of infection, including the liver; thus, the ovary was considered the primary site of infection.

editor_comments: Primary ovarian hydatid disease represents an exceptionally rare entity (<0.3% of echinococcal cases) that frequently mimics benign or malignant ovarian neoplasms on ultrasonography and pelvic imaging. When encountered in postmenopausal patients, the presence of multiple internal daughter cysts and acoustic shadowing can be mistaken for neoplastic septations and mural nodules.
